summary: A reissue of the first BBN site status report, because the original RFC 235 had many typographical errors. It reports how often ARPANET hosts could be reached and which ones were excluded from daily test logins. It was replaced by RFC 252.

eli5.summary: A fixed copy of a report with too many typos. It says which network computers were working when tested. It was replaced by a newer report.

questions: when did arpanet host reporting begin
subtitle: A corrected ARPANET host status report from September 1971.

tldr.problem: The first site status report (RFC 235) had typographical errors that embarrassed the network community.
tldr.mechanism: BBN reissued it with the errors fixed and added daily test results showing which ARPANET hosts were accessible.
tldr.outcome: This began a series of regular biweekly status reports that tracked host availability on the early network.

facts.value: 5 (Open, Dead, Timed Out, Refused, Half Open)

today: RFC 240 is a Historic document and has been obsoleted by RFC 252. It marks the beginning of regular host status reporting on the ARPANET.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 240 reissues the first ARPANET site status report from BBN. The original RFC 235 contained so many typographical errors that the author, Alex McKenzie, decided to republish it with corrections. BBN committed to issuing these status reports approximately every two weeks thereafter, gathering information from daily automated tests and contact with site operators.
sections.eli5: A researcher had to say sorry for a report with too many typos and printed a clean copy instead.

sections.title: Daily Testing and Host Status
sections.content:
BBN performed daily login tests from the BBN prototype Terminal IMP at a random time each weekday to see which hosts were reachable. The results used five status codes: O for Open (host responded and was accessible), D for Dead (unreachable), T for Timed Out (no response within the timeout), R for Refused (returned a close), and 1/2 O for 1/2 Open (opened a connection but then closed or stopped responding).

Some hosts were excluded from daily testing: those not expected to be network servers for at least a month, such as new PDP-10s at Rand, Stanford, Case, and Carnegie; and hosts intended as users only, including Terminal IMPs and the Network Control Center.
sections.eli5: Testers called each computer every day and marked down if it answered, timed out, or refused the call. Some computers were too new or too special to test every day.

sections.title: Host Predictions and Status Summary
sections.content: For each host, the report included predictions about when it would become a network server, obtained from site operators. Most hosts reported status as either Server or User only. Availability varied widely: UCLA's SIGMA-7 and UCSB's IBM-360/75 were consistently open, while others like UTAH's PDP-10 and SRI's PDP-10 were frequently dead or timed out. MIT's Multics H-645 and Lincoln's IBM-360/67 showed intermittent connectivity.
sections.eli5: Each computer's home site said when it might be ready to talk to others, and the tests showed which ones actually answered the calls.
